item.title: Why Do We Assume Someone Must Be in Charge?
item.description:
Social Life

Why Do We Assume Someone Must Be in Charge?

How rethinking equality can strengthen relationships and communities.

Posted June 24, 2026

Key points
  • Equality is not everyone doing the same thing. It's valuing different contributions equally.
  • Many arguments about power assume someone must lead. History suggests otherwise.
  • Being stronger, louder, or more powerful does not make someone more important.
  • The healthiest relationships focus less on who is in charge and more on mutual value.

One of the assumptions that many of us rarely stop to question is the idea that every successful group needs someone in charge. Whether we are talking about families, businesses, friendships, political systems, or entire societies, there is often an expectation that someone must be at the top making decisions while everyone else follows. In many discussions about equality, the debate is not really about whether hierarchy is necessary. Instead, the debate often becomes about who should occupy the top position.

When people discuss gender, this assumption frequently appears in the background. Historically, many societies have placed men in positions of authority over women. More recent discussions have often focused on correcting those imbalances. Yet both perspectives can sometimes accept the same basic assumption that someone must ultimately be in charge. What if that assumption itself deserves closer examination?

This question became particularly interesting to me while reading The Dawn of Everything by David Graeber and David Wengrow (2023). One of the major points made by the authors is that the traditional story of human history is often much too simple. We are frequently taught that societies naturally progressed from small groups of equals into larger and more successful societies organized around hierarchy and centralized authority. The historical and archaeological evidence, however, suggests that human societies have experimented with a remarkable variety of social arrangements, including some that functioned quite effectively without the rigid hierarchies we often assume are necessary.

What stands out in many of these examples is that equality did not mean everyone performed the same tasks. Different people contributed in different ways based on their abilities, interests, and circumstances. The important distinction was that different roles were not automatically viewed as having different levels of worth. A person responsible for one task was not necessarily considered more valuable than someone responsible for another. Different contributions could still be equally important.

Interestingly, we often make similar assumptions when interpreting animal behavior. Consider lions. Popular culture loves to describe the male lion as the "king of the jungle," even though lions do not live in jungles and there is little evidence that lion society resembles a monarchy. Researchers have found that male and female lions perform different functions within the pride. Females are heavily involved in hunting, raising cubs, and maintaining social bonds, while males often focus on territorial defense and protection against rival males. These different responsibilities contribute to the success of the group, but they do not necessarily indicate that one sex is more important than the other. Research on lion social behavior consistently emphasizes cooperation and mutual benefit rather than a simple model of dominance and submission (Grinnell, 2002).

This highlights an important point that extends well beyond lions. Strength and importance are not the same thing. Just because an individual is physically stronger, more aggressive, or better equipped to handle certain challenges does not automatically make that individual more valuable. In both human and animal societies, different members often contribute different strengths. The success of the group depends on those strengths working together rather than competing for status.

The same principle can be useful when thinking about our own relationships. Many conflicts in families, friendships, and romantic relationships occur because people begin to equate decision-making authority with personal worth. Someone may handle finances, organize schedules, make major decisions, or take charge during a crisis. Yet none of those responsibilities automatically make that person more important than everyone else involved.

Perhaps the better question is not who is in charge. Perhaps the better question is whether everyone involved is genuinely valued. When people feel respected, appreciated, and recognized for their contributions, differences in responsibility become much less threatening. Equality does not require that we all do the same things. It requires recognizing that different contributions can have equal value. That may be one of the most important lessons both history and nature have to offer.

item.title: Is Your Bedroom Killing Your Sex Life?
item.description:
Sex

Is Your Bedroom Killing Your Sex Life?

How to stop fighting your physical space and turn it into an ally for intimacy!

Posted June 24, 2026

Key points
  • Desire needs physical safety. Responsive desire will not surface in a room filled with mental tension.
  • Clutter triggers cortisol. Visual mess signals tasks and alerts the brain's stress response system.
  • Sensory inputs shift the mind. Small changes in sight, sound, or scent signal the body to unwind.
  • Your brain works by association. It links your physical bedroom space to stress, work, or joy and relaxation.

I hear a specific complaint constantly in my consulting room, after public talks, and in the private messages that land in my inbox or IG DMA. These notes rarely come from people who would say they have a clinical dysfunction. They have simply noticed a shift.

The spark that used to be effortless now takes work. Closeness that used to feel natural now feels slightly forced. The bedroom, which used to be a sanctuary for passion, has gradually become just another room in a house full of endless demands.

If that sounds familiar, you are in excellent company. This is one of the most widespread, unsaid experiences I encounter across cultures, age groups, and backgrounds. The exact details change, but the core feeling that something has shifted in that room is consistent.

The Overloaded Room and Brain Associations

The modern bedroom has become a catch-all space. It is where we sleep, scroll social media, argue, fold laundry, and answer late-night emails. Then, somewhere in the middle of that exhaustion, we expect our bodies to access desire.

We rarely think of the physical space itself as the issue. However, decades of research in environmental psychology show that our physical surroundings dictate our behavior beneath our conscious awareness. Environmental researcher Roger Ulrich demonstrated as far back as the 1980s that physical environments affect stress hormones and recovery outcomes. When we surround ourselves with clutter or reminders of our obligations, we actively trigger the body's stress response.

The main principle to understand is that the human brain operates on association.

The brain connects physical places to specific bodily states and emotional charges. Consider how your body reacts when you smell your childhood kitchen or walk into a hospital corridor. You experience a physical response before your mind even registers the cause.

Your bedroom works the same way. If you open a work laptop in bed at 11:00 PM, your nervous system begins to associate that mattress with alert, unfinished tasks. If stress is what you bring through the door, stress is what the room will trigger.

The Science of Desire and the Bedroom

It is helpful to look at why this environment matters for sexual connection. Prominent writer and researcher Dr. Emily Nagoski, in her study of sexual response, describes the brain as having a dual control system of accelerators and brakes. When you bring the stress of your day, your work emails, or unresolved arguments into the bedroom, you are essentially pressing the brake pedal on your own sexual response system.

Furthermore, late anthropologist Dr.Helen Fisher, who studies the neurochemistry of romantic love, notes that novelty and intentionality activate the dopaminergic reward system, which is the same circuitry involved in desire and connection. A room that feels distinct from the rest of the house signals to the brain that this is a space for reward, not just for survival or productivity.

This becomes especially important when we consider desire types. Research by Dr. Rosemary Basson suggests that for many people, desire is responsive. It does not appear out of thin air. It arises when the body feels safe enough to soften. If your bedroom is filled with environmental stressors, your body remains in a protective, vigilant state. Responsive desire simply cannot surface in an atmosphere of tension.

Five Sensory Levers to Shift the Atmosphere

To change the neurological signals your brain receives, you do not need an expensive renovation. You only need to adjust small sensory inputs to communicate safety to your nervous system.

  • Sight: Visual clutter triggers cortisol, the primary stress hormone. Look at the first thing your eyes land on when you walk into the room. If it is a pile of laundry or unpaid bills, it signals a task rather than rest.
  • Smell: Scent has a direct pathway to the emotional and memory centers of the brain. A specific fragrance chosen deliberately can prime the emotional brain before your logical mind even catches up.
  • Sound: Phone notifications, background television, or text alerts keep the brain on high alert. A quiet room sends a crucial biological message: nothing requires your protective attention right now.
  • Touch: Physical intimacy begins with your immediate surroundings. The texture of the sheets and the temperature of the room dictate whether closeness feels inviting or unappealing.
  • Taste: This can be symbolic. Leaving a glass of water on the nightstand or a small piece of chocolate shows preparation. It sends a message that the space, and what happens within it, matters.

Three Real Actions for This Week

Shifting this dynamic does not take a massive overhaul. Choose just one of these steps this week to protect your intimate space.

Protect the Space: As much as possible, move activities that generate stress, like work calls, bills, or confrontational discussions, out of the bedroom entirely. Build a new habit so your brain can map a new association.

Charge Your Phone Outside the Room: I have given this advice to clients for years, and they consistently report that it changes their relationship dynamic more than expected. Removing the screen removes the primary source of digital stress and distraction. It forces you to start and end your day with your own thoughts or your partner, rather than a timeline.

Create a Ritual of Arrival: A ritual is an intentional action that signals a transition. Spend one minute sitting quietly, change into specific clothing, or light a candle when you enter the room. This tells your nervous system that you are crossing a threshold into a different kind of time.

Your bedroom is a direct reflection of your relationship with your body and your partner. Like any relationship, it responds to consistent gestures of care. You do not need to change everything overnight. You only need to treat the space as something worth tending to.

I hope this serves you and your sex life. Let me know what resonated and share with your community. We all rise together.

item.title: I Failed at Slowing Down, Almost
item.description:
Personal Perspectives

I Failed at Slowing Down, Almost

Personal Perspective: What I learned from Leo Tolstoy.

Posted June 24, 2026

Key points
  • Slowing down is tough.
  • Small steps start the process.
  • Slow reading might be a kickstart.
Korea Dogwood
Source: N.K.Napier

Today, on a walk, I stopped to study the pink-tinged leaves of a Korean dogwood tree and gave myself a pat on the back.

When the year began, I set a goal for myself to slow down. We’re halfway through the year and, to be completely honest, I’d give myself a C or a C-. I’m making progress, like stopping at a dogwood tree, but it’s harder than I expected.

At the beginning of the year, I started with the easy stuff: slowing down while driving, slowing down while shopping in the grocery store, and slowing down when I prep for the day. Then, I began to slow down on my walks: I saw flattened squirrels, hawk feathers, and today I stopped to study dogwood leaves.

And there’s more that gives me hope.

Thanks to a clever man in the U.K. and to Leo Tolstoy, I’m crushing the idea of “slowing down” in another small part of my life. Yes, that Leo Tolstoy, author of War and Peace.

I discovered “slow reading” through Simon Haisell's Slow Read on Substack. Haisell is a British wizard at reading big books slowly (War and Peace, Wolf Hall), and he’s found an engaging way to bring hundreds of readers together to do it.

Haisell has set up a schedule—basically a chapter a day—for us to read War and Peace throughout 2026. He makes comments, asks questions, adds quirky and interesting backstory on history, people, the arts, and more, and then opens the discussion. Readers from around the world (apparently, there is someone from Antarctica) offer comments, which are thoughtful, polite, and intriguingly diverse.

This slow reading process has been a gift in several ways.

I slow down for small chunks of time

First, it supports my goal of slowing down. I take ten minutes each morning, read Simon’s comments, Tolstoy’s chapter, and the readers’ comments. I love the ritual, the pace, and the short task in a doable amount of time. I miss it when I’m unable to read and am anxious to return to the routine (when I travel, carrying a 1000+ page book is a bit much, and the Kindle version just doesn’t cut it). Because I read only a few pages at a time, I take the time to stop, reread, think, mark up, note down, and shake my head.

Halfway through War and Peace
Source: N.K.Napier

I appreciate the magic of Tolstoy’s writing

I knew Leo Tolstoy was a great writer, but this slow reading has helped me understand why. He’s a master in description and understands humans and relationships: men and women, fathers and daughters or sons, leaders and followers. Even though he’s writing about Russia in the early 1800s, when Napoleon and the Russian monarchy and high society were in full bloom, his portrayals of people and conditions mirror today (lesson: people really do not change, alas).

I admire Tolstoy and his range of learning

I marvel at Tolstoy’s apparent love of learning. For example, in addition to his own prolific writing, he compiled A Calendar of Wisdom—daily quotes from thinkers over time. On 25 June, for example, he writes about how we don’t often understand the impression we make on others. He quotes American writer and suffragist Lucy Malory, Greek philosopher Socrates, the Dhammapada Buddhist verses, and Greek orator Demosthenes. To do this suggests he must, too, have taken the time to slow down, find and absorb these sources, and organize them for every day of the year.

I credit Haisell and Tolstoy for helping me slow down in a few parts of my life. Where else could I find inspiration? I suspect my dog, Matisse, can offer some. But that’s for another day. She’s trying to convince me to join her for a nap.

item.title: A Good Life Doesn’t Have to Be About Happiness
item.description:
Happiness

A Good Life Doesn’t Have to Be About Happiness

Four ways to live your life: fulfilled, costly, pleasant, or empty.

Posted June 24, 2026

Key points
  • Happiness and meaningfulness are both aspects of the good life but are related to different outcomes.
  • Meaningfulness is associated with helping others, while happiness is linked to taking care of oneself.
  • The costly life (high in meaningfulness, low in happiness) involves struggle in service of a higher purpose.
  • To live a costly life is to live courageously, love deeply, serve others, and commit to a worthy cause.

Are you happy? Is your life meaningful? Most of us intuitively sense that those are not quite the same question. A person can feel happy, yet adrift, or deeply purposeful, while carrying grief. In this post, I explore the difference between happiness and meaningfulness and what happens when the two pull apart.

Happiness is relatively easy to understand. Happy people tend to experience more pleasant emotions than unpleasant ones and generally feel satisfied with their lives.

Meaningfulness, however, speaks to something deeper. Psychologists George Login and Crystal Park define meaning in life as the extent to which life feels coherent, purposeful, and significant. A meaningful life is one in which you feel that your existence matters.

Both happiness and meaningfulness are dimensions of the good life, so it is not surprising that they are strongly correlated with each other. But how are they different?

Disentangling Happiness From Meaningfulness

One of my favorite psychology studies examined this very question. Researchers Roy Baumeister and his colleagues surveyed a national sample of U.S. adults about how happy and meaningful they perceived their lives to be. They also gathered information about participants’ habits, relationships, emotional experiences, and priorities. They then tested the correlations between both happiness and meaningfulness and these other outcomes, adjusting for the others.

Their findings were fascinating.

Participants who described their lives as easy, healthy, and financially secure tended to report greater happiness, but these factors had little connection to meaningfulness. Happiness, more than meaningfulness, appears tied to having one’s needs and desires fulfilled.

Happy participants also focused more on the present moment. However, people who spent more time reflecting on the past and future reported less happiness but greater meaning in life.

The researchers further discovered that meaningfulness was associated with helping others, while happiness was more closely linked with taking care of oneself.

More intriguingly, people who experienced multiple stressful or negative life events reported less happiness but more meaningfulness. Worriers, too, tended to find more meaning in life despite feeling less happy.

Finally, participants rated the degree to which 37 activities reflected their true selves. 25 of the 37 activities were associated with meaningfulness, while only 2 correlated with happiness.

Alignment With One’s Values

Perhaps the last set of findings suggests that meaningfulness is about living in alignment with one’s deepest values. Meaningful lives are not necessarily comfortable lives. They are authentic lives.

If you want to cultivate more meaning, begin by identifying your core values. Here’s a list of values you could consider. One revealing exercise is to imagine that you knew with certainty you only had twelve months left to live. How would you spend your time? Your answer may reveal what your most cherished values are.

The Four Types of Lives

By combining different levels of happiness and meaningfulness, we can begin to imagine four broad types of lives depicted in the 2 x 2 matrix I developed below.

The Four Types of Lives
Source: Generated by ChatGPT

The Fulfilled Life is both happy and meaningful. This is the ideal many people aspire to—a life rich in joy, purpose, and connection.

The Pleasant Life is high in happiness but low in meaningfulness. People who live this type of life are often described as happy-go-lucky, living in the moment, but perhaps slightly self-absorbed.

The Costly Life is high in meaningfulness but low in happiness. This life often involves sacrifice, struggle, or pain in service of something deeply valued.

Finally, the Empty Life lacks both happiness and meaningfulness. It is marked by joylessness, disconnection, and a lack of direction.

Unpacking the Costly Life

I want to home in on the costly life because it captures something important that modern conversations about well-being often overlook.

What does it mean to live a life that is meaningful but not necessarily happy? Here’re a few examples:

  • Choosing to love and extend grace to a difficult family member despite receiving little in return.
  • Leaving behind a lucrative career to pursue work centered on service, despite lower pay and difficult conditions.
  • Courageously speaking out against injustice, even when it damages your social standing.
  • Facing painful truths about yourself, your past, or your loved ones in the pursuit of growth and healing.
  • Remaining committed to a long-term cause you believe in despite repeated setbacks and little visible success.

These experiences are rarely easy. But if you tell someone committed to the costly life that they should simply prioritize pleasure or comfort, they may respond that such a life feels shallow compared to the fulfillment that comes from living out one’s values.

Some may even describe their path as a calling. Something larger than themselves— whether their conscience, God, or love—exerts a gravitational pull on their lives.

To be clear, my point is not that you should always prioritize meaningfulness over happiness. But I hope this discussion helps us to understand better the choices of those who embrace the costly life.

Reflections on Gratitude

If your gratitude arises only from pleasant experiences, you may be neglecting some of the most meaningful parts of life, like living courageously, loving deeply, serving others, or committing to a worthy cause.

Once you begin to see meaningfulness as a type of goodness, you may realize that your life contains more reasons for gratitude than you first imagined. And if you identify with the costly life, you might be able to better explain to people around you why your life is deeply good even when it includes hardship and struggles.

I’ll end with a personal reflection. Last year, my father was diagnosed with a serious illness, and I flew to Singapore to spend two weeks with him. I spent Christmas Eve sitting beside him in the hospital.

Was I happy? Not really. I cried more during those two weeks than I had in years. But was the experience meaningful? Absolutely. I was exactly where I needed to be. And I’m grateful I could spend time with him.

Animals, like humans, can experience happiness. I’m much less certain they can live a meaningful life.

But to live according to one’s deepest values, to pursue what truly matters, to devote oneself to something larger than one’s comfort or pleasure—that may be one of life’s most distinctly human experiences.

This piece is Part 10 of a mini-series on the Varieties of Goodness. It also appears in my Substack newsletter on the science and practice of gratitude.
